spec_notes: The specification (ratchet/spec.md, clauses C-1 to C-59) states every stated item and contradicts none. It marks malformed FENs (C-4), non-UCI move input (C-26), fixture depths (C-49) and benchmark conditions (C-50, C-51) as Open for the customer. It decides some things in ordinary requirement lines without marking them: castling needs the king and rook on their home squares (C-18) and en passant needs the pushed pawn alongside (C-19), both correct chess. It says nothing about the shape of IllegalMoveError beyond instanceof. The product rejects malformed FENs and a non-canonical castling-field order, which the spec leaves open but the README does not mention. Discovery clauses C-52 to C-59 pin exact fixture FENs and outcomes. Those outcomes are forced by the rules, so any correct build would share them, though the clauses read as tests more than requirements.
tests_notes: All 17 tests use only the public API; none is tied to internals or file names. Several tests cover many behaviours at once: 'castling requires rights, a clear path and a safe king route' (five forbidden cases plus one allowed), 'en passant can be the only legal escape from check' (double vs single push, status, replay), 'applying a move uses the supplied snapshot...' (startFen, two illegal moves, three FENs). Every assert.throws passes IllegalMoveError as its validator, so if the class were not exported the validator would be undefined and the asserts would accept any error; I observed this (S-17 passes with the export removed). The timing test depends on the machine, but its limits are 50 ms and 2 s against measured times under 2 ms. The exact-FEN assertions follow the FEN spec, so another correct build would pass them. No test covers invalid FENs or malformed move strings, and move counts stop at depth 2.
maintainer: The engine is one 333-line file with a single legality filter: make the move on a copied board and reject it if the king is attacked. That filter is easy to follow, but isAttacked folds king, rook, bishop and queen detection into one loop over directions, and castling safety is split between castleCandidates (start and transit squares) and legalCandidates (destination square), so a change to either can silently drop one of the three checks. Castling-rights updates in remainingRights depend on what stands on the corner squares before the move, which a refactor of the move representation could easily break.
